paras: The Locust Point attacks on non-union Black dockworkers were assaults by white crowds on Black men who had taken the places of striking dockworkers at Locust Point, Baltimore, on August 12 and 13, 1900. A crowd bricked a streetcar carrying the replacement workers one night and stoned a gang of fifteen leaving the docks the next, until one of the Black men fired five shots and wounded three white men. The wire story ran in papers across the country as evidence that the Baltimore strike had taken an 'ugly aspect.'

According to the Baltimore wire report, some 2,000 union stevedores had struck the week before, and 'minor disturbances' were occurring daily. Shipping firms filled the strikers' places with non-union Black men, and the local German-language daily Der Deutsche Correspondent described police escorting replacement freight handlers to their steamer.

On the night of Sunday, August 12, a 'big crowd' attacked a streetcar at Locust Point carrying non-union Black workers and bombarded it with bricks and other missiles until police dispersed it. Der Deutsche Correspondent reported that Robert Korll, arrested in a riot on Fort Avenue that evening for throwing stones at Black men, was fined $102.90, and that Anton Borkoski was fined $11.45 for inciting the crowd.

On Monday evening, August 13, a crowd followed fifteen Black men leaving the Baltimore and Ohio docks for several blocks, pelting them with stones and bricks. The local paper said the men, afraid to walk straight to the streetcar line, had tried a roundabout route toward Fort McHenry and were stoned by a band of whites as far as the foot of Allen Street. There, shortly before 7 p.m., one of the Black men drew a revolver and fired five shots into the pursuing crowd of men, women and boys, scattering it.

Three shots struck: Henry Presser, 31, a laborer, in the right arm; Joseph Benesch, 51, a laborer, in the left knee; and Arthur Rayner, 24, in the left hand. None of the wounds was reported as serious. Officers Wm. Heinz and Perry and then 24 police reserves under three sergeants came to the scene, but the shooter and his companions escaped.

Police arrested August Ruhling shortly after the shooting for refusing to make way for officers, and reserves from all districts were ordered to Locust Point. By August 15 Captain Ward had about 40 police posted there in the evening hours, and Der Deutsche Correspondent reported Locust Point quiet, with the non-union men left unmolested. That day police arrested two Black replacement workers, Alfred Harris, 19, and Joseph Lewis, for carrying concealed revolvers, and Harris was held for trial.

Striking freight handlers meeting at Eintracht Hall on August 13 had condemned the Sunday violence against non-union men, and organizer Frank Weber later expressed his deep regret over Monday's events. A union president, Korner, told the paper that the strikers had kept away from all violence but objected that Black men were allowed to carry revolvers. No report of an arrest of the shooter appears in the coverage.

The wire account appeared on August 14 in papers including the Wichita Daily Eagle, Scranton Tribune, Saint Paul Globe, Indianapolis Journal and Birmingham Age-Herald and later in two weeklies. Its headlines centered the strike and the gunfire, from 'STEVEDORE STRIKE IS SERIOUS' to 'USED PISTOL ON STRIKERS' and 'Three Men Wounded by a Negro.' Condensed versions in the Seattle Post-Intelligencer and Corvallis Gazette dropped the second attack, so the shots appeared to come from the streetcar.

Der Deutsche Correspondent described the stoning by whites in detail and noted that it could not be established whether they were strikers. Its headline, however, made the shooting the story: 'Von Negern geschossen' (shot by Negroes), with three Germans as victims of the Black freight handlers who had not belonged to the strikers.

The wire report wrote as though the strikers themselves made both attacks, while the local paper said the identity of the whites could not be established and the union said its members had avoided violence. Spellings of the wounded men's names vary widely in the wire copies; the local paper, which gives ages and addresses, prints Presser, Benesch and Rayner.

reader.title: Locust Point attacks on non-union Black dockworkers
bases: Crowds attacked non-union Black men who had taken strikers' places on the Locust Point docks during a waterfront strike, stoning a streetcar and then a gang of fifteen leaving the docks (A1, A3, A11).

The Baltimore wire report (A1, A5) and an independent local account in Der Deutsche Correspondent (A11, A12) agree on the stoning of the Black workers, the five shots, the three wounded men and the shooter's escape.

accounts.label: Wire report
accounts.gist: Striking stevedores ('they') bombarded a car of non-union colored men and then stoned fifteen leaving the B&O docks; one fired five shots into a following crowd of men, women and boys, wounding three, and fled.

accounts.label: Local German-language paper
accounts.gist: Black workers afraid to walk straight to the streetcar detoured toward Fort McHenry and were stoned by a band of whites to the foot of Allen Street until one fired; whether the whites were strikers could not be established, and the wounded were not strikers.

accounts.label: Union leaders
accounts.gist: The strikers condemned the Sunday violence and said they had kept away from all violence; one president complained that Black replacements carried revolvers.

framing.detail: Papers from Kansas to Delaware ran the Baltimore wire under strike headlines, some putting the shooting first: 'USED PISTOL ON STRIKERS', 'Three Men Wounded by a Negro'.
Der Deutsche Correspondent said a band of whites stoned the Black workers but headlined the three Germans as 'Opfer der schwarzen Frachtverlader' and mocked the 'schwarzen Revolverhelden'.

record_check.record: Striking Baltimore stevedores attacked ... the shooter escaped.
